Before we start

Two disclaimers, then the map

01
This ages fast

Some of what follows is already out of date. Models, apps and hardware all move faster than a slide deck. The shape of it holds. Treat this deck as an entry point rather than a reference.

02
Every number is an order of magnitude

Not a benchmark. Architectures differ, machines differ, and the same model on two laptops will not behave the same. The figures are here to make the relationships visible. For real numbers, read the official docs, or measure your own machine.

00
Section 00

What it is, and why bother

First, what a “local model” actually is. Then the harder question: cloud AI is good, cheap and everywhere — so why run one on your own machine at all?

00 — What is a local LLM?

A file of numbers, and a program that reads it

A language model whose inference — the arithmetic that produces each word — runs on hardware you own. In practice that means an open-weight model, because someone has to publish the file before you can hold it. It is the same kind of model as the one in the browser tab. What changes is the address.

01

The weights

One file you download once. A few billion numbers, learned during training and then frozen. Nothing about it changes as you use it.

GEMMA-3-1B-IT-Q4_0.GGUF · 720 MB
02

The runner

An ordinary desktop app that loads that file into memory and does the multiplication. LM Studio here; the engine underneath is llama.cpp.

INSTALLS LIKE ANY OTHER APP
03

Your memory

The file has to fit in RAM or VRAM, and is read end to end for every word it writes. That is why the next two hours are mostly about memory.

CAPACITY → FITS · BANDWIDTH → SPEED
Cloud your text→ the internet→ someone’s datacentre→ an answer
Local your text→ your RAM→ an answer

Open weights are not the same as open source. You get the finished numbers to keep, run and fine-tune. The training data and the code that made them usually stay private, and a license can still restrict what you do with the output. Read the model card.

00 — Why bother?

Five reasons that survive scrutiny

01 Privacy Nothing ever leaves the machine
02 Offline Works on a plane
03 No limits No rate limits, no meter
04 Control Swap models. Keep the one you like.
05 Unfiltered No refusals on legitimate work

Take plain LM Studio, not LM Studio Bionic. Bionic is a second, separate app from the same team — a coding and document agent that runs on top of a model, and it can point at open models in the cloud as well as local ones, so it is not automatically offline the way this app is. It is not a newer version of this one; the two are meant to be installed side by side. We want the app that downloads and runs the model.

01 — First win

Load it, say hello, then try to break it.

1Pick your model in the bar along the top and wait for it to load 2Change nothing — the defaults are what we want 3Say hi, and watch the words arrive one at a time 4Then work down this list
Good at this

Write a four-line poem about waiting for a download.

Short, creative, nothing to get factually wrong. This is the shape it is genuinely best at.
Good at this

I have milk, eggs, half an onion and some stale bread. Give me three things I could make.

You handed it everything it needs. Nothing had to be recalled — only rearranged.
Good at this

Rewrite this so my landlord will take it seriously: hey the tap in the kitchen has been dripping for ages can someone look at it

A text transform. The dullest thing on this slide and the one you will actually use.
Try to break it

How many r's are there in strawberry?

The famous one. It usually says two. It never sees letters — only chunks.
Try to break it

Which is bigger, 9.9 or 9.11?

9.9 is bigger. Models that miss it are reading a version number, where 9.11 comes after 9.9.
Try to break it

A man needs to cross a river with a goat. The boat holds the man and the goat. How many trips?

One. Many models recite the wolf-and-cabbage puzzle they memorised instead of reading yours.

These are famous because they are cheap to check, not because the model is stupid. Frontier models miss several of them too, and the first two are about how text is chopped up before the model ever sees it. That is exactly what the next section opens with.

02
Section 02

What just happened

The one trick underneath it all, the two knobs worth touching, and where the file you just downloaded came from.

02 — What just happened

It only ever does one thing: guess what comes next.

01Chop the text into tokens 02Score every token it knows 03Draw one 04Add it to the end then do it all again
The context — re-read in full, every pass 5 tokens
Scoring  
Six candidates shown — the real list is every token in the vocabulary, around 260,000 of them.

Two things worth watching. It re-reads everything each pass, which is what Section 05 turns into a memory bill. And a token is not a word: watch deeper and drained arrive in two pieces. That is why it cannot count the letters in strawberry.

02 — Sampling

The model never picks a word. It picks from a distribution.

Prompt — “the sky at sunset turns…” Balanced
1.00

Temperature divides every score before the probabilities are worked out. Low temperature makes the leader run away with it; high temperature levels the field until nonsense gets a turn.

02 — Sampling

Two ways to cut the tail off

 

Top-p · counts area4 kept
0.90
Min-p · sets a floor4 kept
0.10
How sure is the model?

Flip between the two and watch the right-hand panel. Min‑p adapts. When the model is sure of itself the floor rises and almost nothing else survives; when it is torn the floor drops and the alternatives live. Top‑p cannot tell the difference.

02 — Where models come from

One site, one file format, a handful of packagers

Hugging Face

Where essentially every open model lives. A “repo” is a folder of files, not a product.

HUGGINGFACE.CO
GGUF

The GGUF file

One self-contained file: the weights plus tokenizer, and usually the chat template. This is what you download.

MLX USES ITS OWN FORMAT
WHO?

Who quantized it

Model authors rarely publish 4‑bit builds. Community packagers do.

BARTOWSKI · UNSLOTH · LMSTUDIO‑COMMUNITY · MLX‑COMMUNITY

The name in the search box is not the whole story. One model produces dozens of files at different quantizations, and picking the right one is the skill.

02 — Under the hood

The engines doing the actual work

llama.cpp

The engine almost everything runs on. C++, no dependencies, runs on anything from a Raspberry Pi to a server. Reads GGUF.

EVERY PLATFORM

MLX

Apple’s own array framework, built for unified memory. Meaningfully faster than llama.cpp on a Mac, useless anywhere else.

APPLE SILICON ONLY

Worth knowing because it means the app is not the magic. It is a face on top of an engine, and you can change either one.

02 — Under the hood

If you outgrow LM Studio

Ollama

Terminal-first. One command pulls and runs a model, and it serves an API other apps can talk to.

OLLAMA RUN QWEN3

Open WebUI

A browser front end you self-host, usually pointed at Ollama. Multi-user, and closest to the hosted chat apps.

RUNS IN A BROWSER

Unsloth

Runs your models like the others, and is also the tool people use to train one on their own data.

RUNS AND TRAINS

Same GGUF files underneath, so the model you just downloaded is not wasted — but moving is not quite free. Open WebUI is a front end and needs Ollama (or another server) behind it, and Ollama imports a local GGUF through a Modelfile rather than opening it directly. Unsloth finds what you already have, but installs a Python toolchain to do it, and its interface is still labelled beta.

A Mac has modest compute but wide memory, so it writes quickly and
        thinks slowly. A big discrete GPU is fast at both, for as long as the model fits in
        its VRAM.
        Everything you run here is dense. Every weight is
        active for every token, so active size is simply file size. Section 06 has the
        models where those two part company.

Both machines hold 64 GB, and that is the point: capacity is not
        the number that decides speed. Drag past 16B and watch the PC fall off a cliff the
        Mac does not have. Then drop to 4‑bit and watch the cliff move.
        Weights only. The bars count nothing but the model. So the
        opening state, 32 GB of weights in 32 GB of VRAM, is the theoretical
        edge rather than a configuration to copy: the KV cache of §5 and a couple of
        gigabytes of runtime have to live there too, and in practice that machine falls
        off this cliff a little before the slider says it does.

        The asymmetry
        The Mac is 2.2× behind on writing —
          and 11.6× behind on reading.
      


      
Prefill is arithmetic; decode is memory traffic.
        The 5090 has roughly three times the Mac's bandwidth but around five times its
        peak matrix compute, so which phase you are in decides how big the gap feels.
        The measured prefill gap is wider still, because llama.cpp's CUDA path is mature
        while, on the build these figures were taken from, its Metal path did not yet use
        the matrix units built into the M5 GPU (Apple calls them Neural
        Accelerators; they are not the separate Neural Engine, which this path does not
        touch). That is a version question and it is moving — check what your own
        build does before quoting the gap. Every rate here is an
        order‑of‑magnitude estimate for one 8 B model at 4‑bit
        rather than a benchmark of your machine. Only the clock is real. Attention is
        also quadratic, so a really long prompt is worse than this straight line
        suggests.

        Why bother

Note the shared scale. A quant does not store 24 tiny numbers — it
        stores 24 tiny integers plus one full-precision multiplier for the block. That
        multiplier is why a “4‑bit” file is never exactly 4 bits per weight, and real
        GGUF blocks carry more metadata than this one. Hold that thought for one slide.

Small models fall further. A 30B has parameters to
        spare and shrugs off rounding; a 1B does not, which matters here because a 1B is
        what most of you downloaded. Below 4‑bit the failure is invisible —
        no error, no warning, just quiet loops, contradictions and confident nonsense.
        Shape of the curve: real. Exact percentages: illustrative, and they move with every
        model and benchmark.

GQA is why your arithmetic will over-estimate. The naive
        formula gives every attention head its own key and value; modern models share one KV
        head between groups of them, cutting the cache several-fold. Toggle it and watch the
        line pivot. Some models cut further still with sliding-window layers, which cap the
        cache instead of growing it.

This is why a million tokens is a hardware problem, not a
        setting. Drag to the far right: the cache dwarfs the model it belongs to, and
        no consumer machine holds it. Frontier providers do it with paged caches, aggressive KV
        quantization, sliding windows and racks of accelerators. On your laptop, the honest
        move is to set the context you actually need. LM Studio hands you that slider,
        and now you know what it costs.

            starting with the model on your laptop.

          

            Runs on a laptop
            Open weights, too big

            Estimate, disputed

Nobody outside the lab knows the closed numbers.
        Open-weight vendors publish theirs. The closed labs stopped: OpenAI’s last
        real number was GPT‑3’s and Google’s was PaLM’s, both
        superseded by 2023 releases that gave no figure at all — and Anthropic
        never published one.
        The closed-weight bars are inference rather than fact: the two published attempts
        to measure them from the outside disagree by roughly six times, which is
        why they are drawn as ranges. The lesson survives the uncertainty. Even the
        floor of the most conservative estimate is fifty times the largest model
        a laptop can hold, and over a thousand times the one you downloaded. Note
        too that the dot on each bar is what actually runs per token: a sparse
        model holds the whole total in memory but reads only that slice for each word.
        Memory is set by the big number, speed by the small one —
        which is the one place section 03’s formula forks. Not
        a problem here: everything on the download slide is dense, so the two numbers
        are the same. But it is why a sparse model can feel
        faster than its file size says it has any right to.

    

  

  
  
  

    

      
06 — Good at / bad at

      
What a small model is actually for


      

        

          Give it this
          

            
            
            
            
            
            
          

        

        

          Not this
          

            
            
            
          

        

        
      


      

        

        
        
 

      


      
The pattern is one line: bring the knowledge to the
        model. Everything on the left hands it the material; everything on the
        right asks it to supply the material itself. That is why retrieval over your own
        files works far better than a 1 B model has any right to, and why
        “what do you know about …” disappoints. The right
        column is a difference of degree, not of kind — frontier models
        still hallucinate on 3–19% of fact-seeking questions depending on the model
        and the task, and error still compounds across a long run for everyone. A small
        model just reaches the edge sooner, and says nothing when it gets there.

        grab. The 1‑bit files (*-Q1_0.gguf) are
        merged upstream and run on any recent llama.cpp. Ternary is unsettled: PrismML’s
        own docs say it still needs their fork and that Ollama cannot load it, while their
        demo repo says the group‑64 build (*-Q2_0_g64.gguf)
        is already in mainline. Check the machine you are presenting from, on the night.
        The decode figure is §3’s formula on a published bandwidth, so it is a
        ceiling: PrismML measure 82 tok/s on an M4 Pro and 27 on an
        iPhone 17 Pro Max, roughly half to four fifths of it.

    

  

  
  
  

    

      
07 — Diffusion

      
What if it stopped writing left to right?


      

        
        Both lanes at 2.5× slow motion · same slowdown, so
          the ratio on screen is the real one
      


      

        

          

            

              Autoregressive
              Every model you ran today
            

            
0.00s

          

          
          

            Per pass1 token
            Rate≈250 tok/s
            Passes0
          

        


        

          

            

              Diffusion
              DiffusionGemma · Google DeepMind, Jun 2026
            

            
0.00s

          

          
          

            Per pass256 tokens
            Rate>1,000 tok/s
            Passes0
          

        

      


      

        Where the bottleneck went
        Autoregressive decode reads every weight once
          per token. Diffusion reads them once per denoising pass, and one
          pass moves all 256 tokens forward — sixteen passes, not 256 — so the
          memory bus stops being the wall, and arithmetic becomes it instead.
      


      
This is the formula from §3 breaking.
        tok/s ≈ bandwidth ÷ model size held all the way through because one pass
        produced one token. Denoise a block instead and one pass advances 256 of them, so
        the same read of the weights buys sixteen tokens rather than one —
        which is why a Mac’s bandwidth advantage would matter less here, and raw
        compute more. The catch is the hardware.
        DiffusionGemma (google/diffusiongemma-26B-A4B-it) is a
        26 B mixture of experts with 3.8 B active, and
        Google put the quantized weights inside 24 GB of VRAM: a 4090‑class
        graphics card. That is a desk, not a lap, and well past anything downloaded here today. Apache 2.0, weights on Hugging Face, and it is served
        on Vertex AI if you want to try it without the card. Rates are Google’s
        figures on a single H100, not on anything in this room.
